There is no searching for a loophole, ... no pretext put forward, no human weakness pleaded. He acknowledges his guilt openly, candidly, and without prevarication” (<hi type="italic">Berleb. Bible</hi>). In response to this candid confession of his sin, Nathan announced to him, <hi type="italic">“The Lord also hath let thy sin pass by </hi>(i.e., forgiven it)<hi type="italic">. Thou wilt not die. Only because by this deed thou hast given the enemies of the Lord occasion to blaspheme, the son that is born unto thee shall die.”</hi> נאץ, inf. abs. Piel, with chirek, because of its similarity in sound to the following perfect (see <hi type="italic">Ewald</hi>, §240, <hi type="italic">c</hi>.). גּם, with which the apodosis commences, belongs to the הבּן which follows, and serves to give emphasis to the expression: “Nevertheless the son” (vid., Ges<hi type="italic">.</hi> §155, 2, <hi type="italic">a</hi>.). David himself had deserved to die as an adulterer and murderer. The Lord remitted the punishment of death, not so much because of his heartfelt repentance, as from His own fatherly grace and compassion, and because of the promise that He had given to David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.7.11-2Sam.7.12">2Sa 7:11-12</reference>), - a promise which rested upon the assumption that David would not altogether fall away from a state of grace, or commit a mortal sin, but that even in the worst cases he would turn to the Lord again and seek forgiveness. The Lord therefore punished him for this sin with the judgments announced in <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.10-2Sam.12.12">2Sa 12:10-12</reference>, as about to break upon him and his house. But as his sin had given occasion to the enemies of the Lord - i.e., not only to the heathen, but also to the unbelieving among the Israelites themselves - to blaspheme or ridicule his religion and that of all other believers also, the child that was begotten in adultery and had just been born should die; in order, on the one hand, that the father should atone for his adultery in the death of the son, and, on the other hand, that the visible occasion for any further blasphemy should be taken away: so that David was not only to feel the pain of punishment in the death of his son, but was also to discern in it a distinct token of the grace of God. <div eID="gen4394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4395" type="x-p"/> David’s Penitential Grief, and the Birth of Solomon. - 2Sa 12:15. The last-mentioned punishment was inflicted without delay. When Nathan had gone home, the Lord smote the child, so that it became very ill.
entries.4540510660a7c71daf6fc7939cfa2e4b82622165: <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.16-2Sam.12.17">2Sa 12:16-17</reference> <div eID="gen4395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4396" type="x-p"/> Then David sought God (in prayer) for the boy, and fasted, and went and lay all night upon the earth. וּבא, <hi type="italic">“he came,”</hi> not into the sanctuary of the Lord (<reference osisRef="2Sam.12.20">2Sa 12:20</reference> is proof to the contrary), but into his house, or into his chamber, to pour out his heart before God, and bend beneath His chastising hand, and refused the appeal of his most confidential servants, who tried to raise him up, and strengthen him with food. <hi type="italic">“The elders of his house,”</hi> judging from <reference osisRef="Gen.24.2">Gen 24:2</reference>, were the oldest and most confidential servants, “the most highly honoured of his servants, and those who had the greatest influence with him” (Clericus).
entries.ac1d7749b7318ebb623f644293cfc2b1170e4412: <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.18">2Sa 12:18</reference> <div eID="gen4396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4397" type="x-p"/> On the seventh day, when the child died, the servants of David were afraid to tell him of its death; for they said (to one another), “Behold, while the child was still living, we spoke to him, and he did not hearken to our voice; how should we say to him, now the child is dead, that he should do harm?” (i.e., do himself an injury in the depth of his anguish.)
entries.b154bc816b924eddb8097fb07a02a70a28b25359: <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.19-2Sam.12.20">2Sa 12:19-20</reference> <div eID="gen4397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4398" type="x-p"/> David saw at once what had happened from their whispering conversation, and asked whether the child was dead. When they answered in the affirmative, he rose up from the ground, washed and anointed himself, and changed his clothes; that is to say, he laid aside all the signs of penitential grief and mourning, went into the house of the Lord (the holy tent upon Mount Zion) and worshipped, and then returned to his house, and had food set before him.
entries.d7453397aaeb0410183b1b8a1af5ffd6f73314a6: <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.21-2Sam.12.22">2Sa 12:21-22</reference> <div eID="gen4398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4399" type="x-p"/> When his servants expressed their astonishment at all this, David replied, <hi type="italic">“As long as the boy lived, I fasted and wept: for I thought </hi>(said), <hi type="italic">Perhaps </hi>(who knows) <hi type="italic">the Lord may be gracious to me, that the child may remain alive. But now he is dead, why should I fast? can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he will not return to me.”</hi> On this O. v. Gerlach has the following admirable remarks: “In the case of a man whose penitence was so earnest and so deep, the prayer for the preservation of his child must have sprung from some other source than excessive love of any created object. His great desire was to avert the stroke, as a sign of the wrath of God, in the hope that he might be able to discern, in the preservation of the child, a proof of divine favour consequent upon the restoration of his fellowship with God. But when the child was dead, he humbled himself under the mighty hand of God, and rested satisfied with His grace, without giving himself up to fruitless pain.” This state of mind is fully explained in Ps 51, though his servants could not comprehend it. The form יחנּני is the imperfect <hi type="italic">Kal</hi>, יחנּני according to the <hi type="italic">Chethibh</hi>, though the Masoretes have substituted as the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> וחנּני, the perfect with <hi type="italic">vav consec</hi>.
entries.03e95569bfc60ceb406d46e08ecb7215f5c54935: <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.23-2Sam.12.25">2Sa 12:23-25</reference> <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="2Sam.12.23">2Sa 12:23</reference></hi> is paraphrased very correctly by Clericus: “I shall go to the dead, the dead will not come to me.” - 2Sa 12:24. David then comforted his wife Bathsheba, and lived with her again; and she bare a son, whom he called <hi type="italic">Solomon</hi>, the man of peace (cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.9">1Ch 22:9</reference>). David gave the child this name, because he regarded his birth as a pledge that he should now become a partaker again of peace with God, and not from any reference to the fact that the war with the Ammonites was over, and peace prevailed when he was born; although in all probability Solomon was not born till after the capture of Rabbah and the termination of the Ammonitish war. His birth is mentioned here simply because of its connection with what immediately precedes. The writer adds (in <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.24">2Sa 12:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.25">2Sa 12:25</reference>), <hi type="italic">“And Jehovah loved him, and sent by the hand </hi>(through the medium)<hi type="italic">of Nathan the prophet; and he called his son Jedidiah</hi> (i.e., beloved of Jehovah), <hi type="italic">for Jehovah’s sake.”</hi> The subject to ויּשׁלח (he sent) cannot be David, because this would not yield any appropriate sense, but must be <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>, the subject of the clause immediately preceding. “To send by the hand,” i.e., to make a mission by a person (vid., <reference osisRef="Exod.4.13">Exo 4:13</reference>, etc.), is equivalent to having a commission performed by a person, or entrusting a person with a commission to another. We learn from what follows, in what the commission with which Jehovah entrusted Nathan consisted: <hi type="italic">“And he </hi>(Nathan, not Jehovah)<hi type="italic">called his </hi>(the boy’s) <hi type="italic">name Jedidiah.”</hi> And if Nathan is the subject to “called,” there is nothing to astonish in the expression “because of the Lord.” The idea is this: Nathan came to David according to Jehovah’s instructions, and gave Solomon the name <hi type="italic">Jedidiah</hi> for Jehovah’s sake, i.e., because Jehovah loved him. The giving of such a name was a practical declaration on the part of Jehovah that He loved Solomon, from which David could and was intended to discern that the Lord had blessed his marriage with Bathsheba. <hi type="italic">Jedidiah</hi>, therefore, was not actually adopted as Solomon’s name.
entries.fa1682e497d3285416f8e6e5aeb128a45cb5da4a: <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.26-2Sam.12.28">2Sa 12:26-28</reference> <div eID="gen4399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4400" type="x-p"/> Conquest of Rabbah, and Punishment of the Ammonites (comp. <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.1-1Chr.20.3">1Ch 20:1-3</reference>). - <hi type="italic">“Joab fought against Rabbah of the children of Ammon, and took the king’s city.”</hi> המּלוּכה עיר, the capital of the kingdom, is the city with the exception of the acropolis, as <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.27">2Sa 12:27</reference> clearly shows, where the captured city is called “the water-city.” <hi type="italic">Rabbah</hi> was situated, as the ruins of <hi type="italic">Ammân</hi> show, on both banks of the river (<hi type="italic">Moiet</hi>) <hi type="italic">Ammân</hi> (the upper Jabbok), in a valley which is shut in upon the north and south by two bare ranges of hills of moderate height, and is not more than 200 paces in breadth. “The northern height is crowned by the castle, the ancient acropolis, which stands on the north-western side of the city, and commands the whole city” (see Burckhardt, <hi type="italic">Syria</hi> ii. pp. 612ff., and Ritter, <hi type="italic">Erdkunde</hi> xv. pp. 1145ff.). After taking the water-city, Joab sent messengers to David, to inform him of the result of the siege, and say to him, <hi type="italic">“Gather the rest of the people together, and besiege the city</hi> (i.e., the acropolis, which may have been peculiarly strong), <hi type="italic">and take it, that I may not take the city </hi>(also),<hi type="italic">and my name be named upon it,”</hi> i.e., the glory of the conquest be ascribed to me. Luther adopts this explanation in his free rendering, “and I have a name from it.”
entries.c4257a9b75eb3c233f144d155bd2c0c552b27ba2: <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.29">2Sa 12:29</reference> <div eID="gen4400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4401" type="x-p"/> Accordingly David <hi type="italic">“gathered together all the people,”</hi> - i.e., all the men of war who had remained behind in the land; from which we may see that Joab’s besieging army had been considerably weakened during the long siege, and at the capture of the water-city, - <hi type="italic">“and fought against the acropolis, and took it.”</hi>
entries.52ce0d6eb4e8a79674e7563265967060e78a2e39: <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.30">2Sa 12:30</reference> <div eID="gen4401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4402" type="x-p"/> He then took their king’s crown (<hi type="italic">“their king,”</hi> viz., the king of the Ammonites) from off his (the king’s) head; so that he had either been taken prisoner or slain at the capture of the city. The weight of the crown was <hi type="italic">“a talent of gold, and precious stones”</hi> (sc., were upon it): as the writer of the Chronicles has correctly explained it by supplying בּהּ. The Hebrew talent (equal to 3000 shekels) was 83 1/2 Dresden pounds. But the strongest man could hardly have borne a crown of this weight upon his head for however short a time; and David could scarcely have placed it upon his own head. We must therefore assume that the account of the weight is not founded upon actual weighing, but simply upon an approximative estimate, which is somewhat too high. David also took a great quantity of booty out of the city. 1 Sa 12:31 <div eID="gen4402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4403" type="x-p"/> He also had the inhabitants executed, and that with cruel tortures. <hi type="italic">“He sawed them in pieces with the saw and with iron harrows.”</hi> בּמּגרה ויּשׂם, “he put them into the saw,” does not give any appropriate sense; and there can be no doubt, that instead of וישׂם we should read ויּשׂר (from שׂוּר): “he cut (sawed) them in pieces.” הבּרזל וּבמגזרות, <hi type="italic">“and with iron cutting tools.”</hi> The meaning of the ἁπ. λεγ. מגזרות cannot be more precisely determined. The current rendering, “axes or hatchets,” is simply founded upon the circumstance that גּזר, to cut, is applied in 2Ki 6:4 to the felling of trees. The reading in the Chronicles, וּבמּגרות, is evidently a copyist’s error, as we have already had בּמּגרה, “with the saw.” The meaning of the next clause is a disputed point, as the reading itself varies, and the Masoretes read בּמּלבּן instead of the <hi type="italic">Chethibh</hi> במלכן, “he made them go through brick-kilns,” i.e., burnt them in brick-kilns, as the lxx and Vulgate render it. On the other hand, Thenius takes the <hi type="italic">Chethibh</hi> under his protection, and adopts Kimchi’s explanation: “he led them through <hi type="italic">Malchan</hi>, i.e., through the place where the Ammonites burned their children in honour of their idol.” Thenius would therefore alter בּמלכּם into בּמלכּם or בּמּלכּם: “he offered them as sacrifices in their image of Moloch. ” But this explanation cannot be even grammatically sustained, to say nothing of the arbitrary character of the alteration proposed; for the technical expression למּלך בּאשׁ חעביר, “to cause to go through the fire for Moloch” (<reference osisRef="Lev.18.21">Lev 18:21</reference>), is essentially different from בּמּלך חעביר, to cause to pass through Moloch, an expression that we never meet with. Moreover, it is impossible to see how burning the Ammonites in the image of Moloch could possibly be “an obvious mode of punishing idolatry,” since the idolatry itself consisted in the fact that the Ammonites burned their children to Moloch. So far as the circumstances themselves are concerned, the cruelties inflicted upon the prisoners are not to be softened down, as Daaz and others propose, by an arbitrary perversion of the words into a mere sentence to hard labour, such as sawing wood, burning bricks, etc. At the same time, the words of the text do not affirm that <hi type="italic">all</hi> the inhabitants of Rabbah were put to death in this cruel manner. בּהּ אשׁר העם (without כּל) refers no doubt simply to the fighting men that were taken prisoners, or at the most to the male population of the acropolis of Rabbah, who probably consisted of fighting men only. In doing this, David merely retaliated upon the Ammonites the cruelties with which they had treated their foes; since according to <reference osisRef="Amos.1.13">Amo 1:13</reference> they ripped up women who were with child, and according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.11.2">1Sa 11:2</reference> their king Nahash would only make peace with the inhabitants of Jabesh upon the condition that the right eye of every one of them should be put out. It is sufficiently evident from this, that the Ammonites had aimed at the most shameful extermination of the Israelites. <hi type="italic">“Thus did he unto all the cities of the Ammonites,”</hi> i.e., to all the fortified cities that resisted the Israelites. After the close of this war, David returned to Jerusalem with all the men of war. The war with the Syrians and Ammonites, including as it did the Edomitish war as well, was the fiercest in which David was ever engaged, and was also the last great war of his life.  <chapter eID="2Sam.12"/> <div eID="gen4403" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XII.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p>AND the LORD sent Nathan <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The Prophet, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 7. 2. 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 1. 8. When the or<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dinary means did not awaken <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> to Repentance, God useth an Extraordinary Course. Thus the Merciful God pi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ties and prevents him who had so horribly forsaken and forgotten God.</ns0:note> unto David: and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psa. 51. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:note> he came unto him, and said unto him, There were two men in one city <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">He prudently ushereth in his Reproof with a Parable, after the manner of the Eastern Nations, and ancient times, that so he might surprize <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> and cause him unawares to give Sentence against himself. He manageth his Relation as if it had been a real thing; and demands the King's Justice in the case. Though the Appli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cation of this Parable to <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> be easie and obvious, yet it matters not, if some circumstances be not so applicable; because it was fit to put in some such Clauses, either for the decency of the Parable, or that <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> might not too early discover his Design.</ns0:note>; the one rich and the other poor:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:255" />2 The rich <ns0:hi>man</ns0:hi> had exceeding many flocks and herds <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Noting <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s many Wives and Concubines.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 But the poor <ns0:hi>man</ns0:hi> had nothing save one lit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tle ew<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>lamb <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Designing <ns0:hi>Uriah,</ns0:hi> with his own and onely Wife.</ns0:note>, which he had bought <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">As men then used to buy their Wives: or, <ns0:hi>had procured.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> and nou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rished up: and it grew up together with him, and with his children, it did eat of his own <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> Morsel.</ns0:note> meat, and drank of his own cup, and lay in his bosome <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Which <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> might take for Hyperbolical Expressions of his tender care of, and affection to it. Although there want not Instances of some who have treated such Brute-Creatures in this manner.</ns0:note>, and was unto him as a daughter.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 And there came a traveller <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">This some make to be the Devil; whom <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> grati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fied by his Sin; but it rather seems added for the decency of the Parable.</ns0:note> unto the rich man, and he spared to take of his own flock, and of his own herd, to dress for the wayfaring man that was come unto him, but took the poor mans lamb, and dressed it for the man that was come to him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 And Davids anger was kindled greatly against the man, and he said to Nathan, <ns0:hi>As</ns0:hi> the LORD liveth, the man that hath done this <ns0:hi>thing,</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> is worthy to die.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the Son of death.</ns0:note> shall surely die <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">This seems to be more than the Fact deserved, or than he had Commission to Inflict for it, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 22. 1. But it is observable, That <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> now when he was most Indulgent to himself, and to his own Sin, was most severe to others; as appears by this Passage, and the following Relation <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 31. which was done in the time of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s impenitent continu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ance in his Sin.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 And he shall restore the lamb <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 22. 4.</ns0:note> fourfold, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause he did this thing, and because he had no pity.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 And Nathan said to David, Thou <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> the man <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Thou hast committed this Crime with great Aggravati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ons; and out of thine own mouth thy Sentence hath pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceeded, and thou art worthy of Death.</ns0:note>. Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Sam. 16. 13.</ns0:note> I anointed thee king over Israel, and I delivered thee out of the hand of Saul:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 And I gave thee thy masters house, and thy masters wives <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>women,</ns0:hi> as that Word is elsewhere used; as <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 31. 18. And though we read not a word of God's giving, or of <ns0:hi>Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vid</ns0:hi>'s taking any of <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s Wives into his bosome; or, which is all one, into his Bed; Yet (which I think to be aimed at here) it might be according to the manner of that time, that the Wives and Concubines of the Precedent King, belonged to the Successor, to be at least at his Dispose. And to pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tend to them, was interpreted little less than pretending to the Crown. Which made it fatal to <ns0:hi>Adonijah</ns0:hi> to ask <ns0:hi>Abi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />shag,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 2. 23 And to <ns0:hi>Abner</ns0:hi> to be suspected for <ns0:hi>Rispah,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 3. 8. And <ns0:hi>Absalon,</ns0:hi> Usurping the Crown, usurped the Concubines also; which is looked on as a Crime unpardona<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble, 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 16. 21. nor would this have been reckoned amongst the Mercies and Blessings which God here is said to give him, and which are opposed to that which he <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>infully took: but we do read, That <ns0:hi>Merab Saul</ns0:hi>'s Daughter, was given to him for his Wife by <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi>'s promise, and consequently by God's grant; though afterwards <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> perfidiously gave her to another Man; and that <ns0:hi>Michal,</ns0:hi> the other Daughter, was actually given to him, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 18. And it is very possible, that some other of <ns0:hi>Davids</ns0:hi> Wives were nearly Related to the House of <ns0:hi>Saul;</ns0:hi> whereby <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> might design to enlarge and strengthen his Interest in the Kingdom. Although there is no absolute Necessity of re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />straining this to <ns0:hi>Saul,</ns0:hi> seeing the Word is Plural, <ns0:hi>Masters;</ns0:hi> and may belong to others also, who sometimes were owned by <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> as his Masters, Lords, or Superiors, such as <ns0:hi>Ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bal</ns0:hi> was, and some others not elsewhere named might be, whose <ns0:hi>Houses</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Wives,</ns0:hi> or, at least, <ns0:hi>Women,</ns0:hi> God might give to <ns0:hi>David.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> into thy bosome, and gave thee the house of Israel and of Judah, and if <ns0:hi>that had been</ns0:hi> too little, I would moreover have given unto thee such and such things <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Such other things as thou hadst wanted, or in reason desired.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 Wherefore hast thou despised the command<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment of the LORD <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Those Laws of God which forbad thee to do this thing, by not giving them that respect and observance which they deserved.</ns0:note>, to do evil in his sight? thou hast killed Uriah the Hittite <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">That Valiant, and Generous, and Noble Person.</ns0:note> with the sword, and hast taken his wife <ns0:hi>to be</ns0:hi> thy wife <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">This he mentions amongst his other Sins; partly, because he had rewarded her, who by God's Law should have been severely punished: partly, because he compassed this Marriage by wicked Practices, even by <ns0:hi>Uriah</ns0:hi>'s Murder, and for sinful ends, even for the gratification of his inor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dinate and sensual Lusts, and for the concealment of that Sin which he was obliged to con<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ess and lament.</ns0:note>, and hast slain him with the sword of the children of Am<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mon <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Those cursed Enemies of God, and of his People, whom thou hast encouraged and hardned in their Idolatry, by giving up him, and others of God's People into their hands. And note here, That although <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> did not kill <ns0:hi>Uriah</ns0:hi> himself, nor command any to do it; but onely that he should be put upon dangerous Service, (which a General of an Army oft doth to Soldiers under him, on justifiable accounts, without be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing therefore Legally chargeable with Murder, though the person so employed dye in the Service:) yet in God's ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />count, who judged of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Design therein, it is justly so reputed. And therefore, though the <ns0:hi>Ammonites</ns0:hi> slew <ns0:hi>Uriah,</ns0:hi> yet <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> is said to have killed him with their Sword.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 Now therefore the sword shall never depart from thine house <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">During the residue of thy Life: as appears from the following History.</ns0:note>, because thou hast despised me, and hast taken the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be thy wife.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 Thus saith the LORD, Behold, I will raise up evil <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">To wit, the evil of Punishment.</ns0:note> against thee out of thine own house <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">From thy own Chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren and Family.</ns0:note>, and I will <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Deut. 28. 30. Chap. 16. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>2.</ns0:note> take thy wives before thine eyes <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Openly, so as thou shalt know it as certainly as if thou didst see it, and yet not be able to hinder it.</ns0:note>, and give <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> I shall by my Providence, give him power over them, which I know he will abuse; and I shall not restrain him from so doing, either by my Grace or Providence.</ns0:note> unto thy neighbour <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">To one who is very near to thee, even thy beloved Son <ns0:hi>Absolom.</ns0:hi> But God expresseth this here darkly and doubt<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fully, that the accomplishment of it might not be hindred.</ns0:note>, and he shall lie with thy wives in the sight of the sun <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">in the open Day, and in a Publick Place. The accom<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plishment hereof, See <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 16. 22.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 For thou didst <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> secretly: but I will do this thing <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> I will Execute this Judgment. This God did by inclining <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Heart to leave his Concubines, to keep his House, and so to come into <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi>'s Power, by giving up <ns0:hi>Achitophel</ns0:hi> to his own Carnal Policy, which readily suggested to him that wicked and desperate Counsel; and by exposing <ns0:hi>Absalom</ns0:hi> to these Temptations, and leaving him to his own Vicious Inclinations, which God certainly knew would in such circumstances produce that Effect. So the Sin was wholly from Men; but the ordering and over-ruling their Mistakes and Miscarriages to this end, was from God.</ns0:note> before all Israel, and before the Sun.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 And David said unto Nathan, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psa. 32. 5. and 51. 4.</ns0:note> I have sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ned against the LORD <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">I now freely confess, that Sin which I have hitherto so wickedly smothered; and I have deserved all these, and far heavier Judgments for it; and I am more troubled for my Sin against my Soveraign Lord and gracious God, than for the shame and punishment that follow it. How serious and pathetical this confession was, we may see, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 51.</ns0:note>. And Nathan said unto David, The LORD also hath put away thy sin <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> So far as concerns thy own Life and Eternal Salvation: both which were forfeited by this Sin.</ns0:note>, thou shalt not die <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">As by thy own Sentence <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 5. thou didst deserve, and as thou mightest ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pect to do by my immediate Stroke; though possibly thou mightest elude the Law, before a humane Judicature, or there be no Superior to Execute the Law upon thee.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:256" />14 Howbeit, because by this deed thou hast gi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven great occasion to the enemies of the LORD to blaspheme <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> To reproach both God and his People, and the true Religion. For though these were not concerned in <ns0:hi>Da<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vid</ns0:hi>'s Sin, the blame and shame of which should have been appropriated to him; yet <ns0:hi>Heathens</ns0:hi> and wicked men would, according to their own evil Minds, and malicious Hearts, fasten the Reproach of this upon God and Religion; as if God were unholy, because the man after God's own heart was so; and partial, in conniving at so great a Crime, when <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> was cast off for a far less Sin: and negligent in the Go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vernment of the World, and of his Church in suffering such a Wickedness, as even <ns0:hi>Heathens</ns0:hi> have abhorred to go un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />punished; and as if all Religion were but Hypocrifie and Imposture, and a pretence for Villanies. Besides, the <ns0:hi>Am<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />monites</ns0:hi> upon their success against <ns0:hi>Uriah</ns0:hi> and his Party, did doubtless magnifie and praise their Idols, and blaspheme the God of Israel.</ns0:note>, the child also <ns0:hi>that is</ns0:hi> born unto thee, shall surely die <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Which, considering his Affection to it, and the Punishment threatned to the poor innocent Infant for his sake, must needs be grievous to him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 And Nathan departed unto his house: and the LORD strook the child <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">With some sudden and dangerous distemper.</ns0:note> that Uriahs wife bare unto David, and it was very sick.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 David therefore besought God for the child <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Supposing the Threatning might be conditional, and so the Execution of it prevented by Prayer.</ns0:note>, and David <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> fasted a <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ast.</ns0:note> fasted, and went in <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">To wit, into his Closet, as <ns0:hi>Matt.</ns0:hi> 6. 6. to pray solitarily and earnestly as he had done with others. Or this Word may onely note his Progress and continuance in the actions here expressed.</ns0:note>, and lay all night upon the earth.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 And the elders of his house <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">The Chief Officers of his Kingdom and Houshold who were there present.</ns0:note> arose, <ns0:hi>and went</ns0:hi> to him, to raise him up from the earth: but he would not, neither did he eat bread with them <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">This excessive Mourning did not pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceed simply from the fear of the loss of the Child; but from a deep sence of his Sin, and from the Divine Displea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sure manifested herein; and particularly, from a just appre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hension of the injury which he had done to the Child by his Sin, which justice obliged him to do his utmost to repair by Prayer, or other means.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 And it came to pass on the seventh day <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Either, 1. From the beginning of the Distemper. Or, rather, 2. From the day of his Birth, which is the most usual way of computation of Mens Days or Years: for it is apparent, that this happened during the time of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Fasting, and lying upon the Earth, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 20. which it is not probable that it lasted for Seven Days.</ns0:note>, that the child died: and the servants of David fea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />red to tell him that the child was dead: for they said <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Whispering among themselves, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 19.</ns0:note>, Behold, while the child was yet alive, we spake unto him, and he would not hearken unto our voice: how will he then <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> do hurt.</ns0:note> vex himself, if we tell him that the child is dead?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 But when David saw that his servants whis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pered, David perceived that the child was dead: therefore David said unto his servants, Is the child dead? And they said, He is dead.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 Then David arose from the earth, and wash<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed, and anointed <ns0:hi>himself,</ns0:hi> and changed his apparel, and came into the house of the LORD <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> To the Tabernacle, to confess his Sin before the Lord, and to own his Justice in this stroke, and the other threatnings, and to deprecate his great and just displeasure, and to acknowledge Gods rich mercy, in sparing his own Life; and to offer such Sacrifices as were proper and re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quired in such cases. Nor did <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> transgress that Law, <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 19. 14. in going thither before the Seven Days were expired. For neither is there the same reason of a Tent, and of a dwelling House, where the several Rooms of the House are as distinct as several Tents; nor is it here said, that <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> was in the same Room, or in the same House where the Child died.</ns0:note>, and wor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />shipped: then he came to his own house, and when he required, they set bread before him, and he did eat.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 Then said his servants unto him, What thing <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> this that thou hast done? thou didst fast and weep for the child <ns0:hi>while it was</ns0:hi> alive, but when the child was dead, thou didst rise and eat bread.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 And he said, While the child was yet alive, I fasted and wept: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">See Isa. 33. 1. Jon. 3. 9.</ns0:note> for I said, Who can tell <ns0:hi>whe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther</ns0:hi> God will be gracious to me, that the child may live <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">For God's threatning of the Child's Death might be conditional, as that was of <ns0:hi>Ninevehs</ns0:hi> Destruction, <ns0:hi>Io<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nah</ns0:hi> 3. 4.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 But now he is dead, wherefore should I fast <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Seeing Fasting and Prayer cannot now prevail with God for his Life.</ns0:note>? can I bring him back again? I shall go to him <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Into the state of the Dead, in which he is, and into Heaven, where I doubt not I shall find him.</ns0:note>, but he shall not return to me.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 And David comforted Bath sheba his wife <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Who was now much dejected, both for her former Sin which she truly Repented of, as may be gathered from <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 31. 1, 2, 3, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> and for the loss of that Child which was very dear to her, and which might seem to be the one<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly tie of <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Affection to her; which being now dead, she might think that <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> would utterly cast her off, and leave her to that Shame and Punishment which she had deserved.</ns0:note>, and went in unto her <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">To wit, into her Chamber or Bed.</ns0:note>, and lay with her: and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matt. 1. 6.</ns0:note> she bare a son and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Chron <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. 9.</ns0:note> he called his name Solo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mon; and the LORD loved him <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The Lord declared to <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> that he loved his Son, notwith<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />standing the just cause which <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> had given to God to alienate his Affections from him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 And he sent by the hand of Nathan the prophet; and he called his name <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">That is, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />loved of the Lord.</ns0:note> Jedidiah, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause of the LORD <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Either, because of the Lord's love to him, as the Name signifies: or because the Lord commanded him to do so.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 And Joab fought against Rabbah of the chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren of Ammon, and took the royal city <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> That part of the City where was the Kings Palace where he ordinarily resided; though now it seems he was re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tired to a strong Fort.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 And Joab sent messengers to David and said, I have fought against Rabbah, and have taken the city of waters <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">The same Royal City so called, because it either stood beside the River, or was encompassed with Water, both for defence and delight. Although the Words are by some Learned Men rendred thus, <ns0:hi>I have taken,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>intercepted,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>cut off water from the city.</ns0:hi> Which well agrees, both with the words, <ns0:hi>eth</ns0:hi> being here put for <ns0:hi>meeth,</ns0:hi> which is frequent; as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 4. 1. and 44. 4. <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 9. 29, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> and with the Relation of <ns0:hi>Iosephus</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Iew,</ns0:hi> who saith, The Conduits of Water were cut off, and so the City was taken; And with a Relation of <ns0:hi>Polybius</ns0:hi> concerning the same Ciry, which was taken afterwards by <ns0:hi>Antiochus</ns0:hi> in the same manner, by cutting off Water from the City.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28 Now therefore, gather the rest of the peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple together, and encamp against the city, and take it <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">For having taken one part of the City, he concluded the remaining part of it could not long stand out.</ns0:note>: lest I take the city, and <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> my name be called upon it.</ns0:note> it be called after my name <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Lest I have the Honour of taking it. Thus he seeks to engrati<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ate himself with the King, by pretending great care for his Honour and Interest.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29 And David gathered all the people toge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Either because <ns0:hi>Ioab</ns0:hi> needed more help for the Storming of the City: or, at least, for the Prosecution of the Victo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry, and Execution of Justice upon the whole Land: or because he would have them all to partake of <ns0:hi>the spoil of the City,</ns0:hi> which was there <ns0:hi>in great abundance, v.</ns0:hi> 30. the rather because they were all exposed to the hazard of utter Ruine, in case the <ns0:hi>Ammonites</ns0:hi> had prevailed against them.</ns0:note>: and went to Rabbah: and fought against it, and took it.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="30">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:256" />30 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Chron. 20. 2.</ns0:note> And he took their kings crown from off his head, (the weight whereof <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> a talent of gold <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Or rather, <ns0:hi>the price whereof,</ns0:hi> &c. For as the Hebrew <ns0:hi>Shekel</ns0:hi> signifies both a Weight, and a piece of Money of a certain price; so also may <ns0:hi>mishkal,</ns0:hi> as proceeding from the same Root. And in general, the same Words both in <ns0:hi>Hebrew, Greek</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Latine,</ns0:hi> are promiscuously used, to signifie either Weight, or Price; as is well known to the Learned. And the addition of <ns0:hi>pretious stones,</ns0:hi> which are never valued by the Weight of Gold, makes this signification here most proper, and probable. Moreover, the Weight might seem too great either for the King of <ns0:hi>Ammon,</ns0:hi> or for <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> to wear it upon his Head. Although, if this were meant of the Weight, it might be said, that this was not a Crown to be worn ordinarily, but meerly to be put on upon the King's Head at his Coronation, or upon Solemn occasions, as here where this was done, in token of the Translation of this Kingdom to <ns0:hi>David;</ns0:hi> and, it may be, it was held up, or sup<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ported by two Officers of State, that it might not be too burdensome to him, and after a little while taken off.</ns0:note>, with the precious stones) and it was <ns0:hi>set</ns0:hi> on Davids head: and he brought forth the spoil of the city <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> very great. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                     </ns0:note> in great abundance.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="31">31 And he brought forth the people that <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> therein <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The words are indefinite, and therefore not necessarily to be understood of all the people; for it had been Barbarous to use Women and Children thus; but of the Men of War, and especially, of those who had been the Chief Actors or Abettors of that Villanous Action against <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Ambassa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dours, which was contrary to the Law of Nature, and of Nations, and of all Humanity, and of the Dreadful War ensuing upon it; for which, they might seem to deserve, the severest Punishments. Although indeed there seems to have been too much Rigour used; especially, because these dread<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful Deaths were Inflicted not onely upon those great Coun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sellors, who were the onely Authors of that vile Usage of the Ambassadours; but upon a great number of the People who were Innocent from that Crime. And therefore it is probably conceived, That <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> exercised this Cruelty whilst his Heart was hardned, and impenitent; and when he was bereaved of that free and good Spirit of God, which would have taught him more Mercy and Moderation.</ns0:note>, and put them under saws <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">He Sawed them to Death: of which Punishment, we have Ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />amples both in Scripture, <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 11. 37. and in other Authors.</ns0:note>, and under harrows of iron, and under axes of iron <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">He caused them to be laid down upon the Ground, and <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>orn by sharp Iron Harrows drawn over them, and hewed in pieces by keen Axes.</ns0:note>, and made them pass through the brick-kiln <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> To be burnt in Brick-kilns. Or, <ns0:hi>made them to pass through the furnace of Malchen: i. e.</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Moloch,</ns0:hi> called also <ns0:hi>Milchom,</ns0:hi> and here <ns0:hi>Malchen;</ns0:hi> Punishing them with their own Sin, and with the same kind of Punishment which they Inflicted upon their own Chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren: See 2 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 16. 3. and 23. 10. and <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 18. 21. and 20. 2. and <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 18. 10.</ns0:note>: and thus did he unto all the cities of the children of Ammon. So David and all the people returned unto Jerusalem.</ns0:p>
